title: Mastering Thyroid Eye Disease (TED)
summary: A comprehensive clinical guide to Graves' Orbitopathy, covering the complex interplay of TSHR/IGF-1R signaling, the Rundle curve of activity, and the multidisciplinary management from Selenium to Teprotumumab and Rehabilitative Surgery.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Thyroid Eye Disease (TED), also known as Graves' Orbitopathy (GO), is an organ-specific autoimmune inflammatory disorder characterized by remodeling of orbital tissues. It is the most common cause of unilateral and bilateral proptosis in adults, primarily associated with Graves' hyperthyroidism, though patients may be euthyroid or hypothyroid.

branches: TSHR & IGF-1R Crosstalk: Synergistic signaling on CD34+ fibroblasts
Glycosaminoglycan (GAG) Production: Hyaluronic acid causes osmotic edema
Adipogenesis: Differentiation of fibroblasts into adipocytes (fat expansion)
Cytokine Storm: IL-1, TNF-alpha, and IF-gamma drive inflammation
Muscle Fibrosis: End-stage cicatricial changes leading to restrictive strabismus

rows: Widened palpebral fissures due to upper lid retraction in primary gaze.
Lid lag: The upper eyelid fails to follow the globe downward on downgaze.
Inability to maintain convergence of the eyes.
Absence of forehead wrinkling on upward gaze.
Staring or frightened expression on active fixation.

sections.title: Clinical Activity Score (CAS)
content: 1. Spontaneous retrobulbar pain
2. Pain on upward or downward gaze
3. Eyelid erythema
4. Conjunctival injection
5. Chemosis (conjunctival edema)
6. Swelling of the caruncle or plica
7. Eyelid edema
Note: Score ≥ 3/7 indicates Active TED.

content.explanation: N: No signs/symptoms; O: Only signs (lid retraction); S: Soft tissue involvement; P: Proptosis; E: Extraocular muscle involvement; C: Corneal involvement; S: Sight loss (Optic Neuropathy).

rows: Minor impact on daily life; lid retraction <2mm; mild soft tissue signs.
Observation, Selenium (100mcg BID), Lubricants, Smoking cessation.
Lid retraction ≥2mm; Proptosis ≥3mm above normal; Diplopia.
Dysthyroid Optic Neuropathy (DON) or Corneal Breakdown.
Emergency IV Steroids or Orbital Decompression Surgery.

sections.title: Imaging Findings: CT and MRI
content: Coke-Bottle Sign: Characteristic spindle-shaped enlargement of muscle bellies.
Tendon Sparing: Unlike orbital myositis, TED spares the muscle tendons.
Increased Orbital Fat: Proliferation and herniation of fat.
Apical Crowding: Compression of the optic nerve at the orbital apex.
MRI T2 Signal: High signal in muscles indicates active inflammatory phase (edema).

content.explanation: Order of muscle involvement: 1. Inferior Rectus (most common); 2. Medial Rectus; 3. Superior Rectus; 4. Lateral Rectus; 5. Obliques (least common).

rows: Painful; involves the muscle tendon; rapid onset.
Diffuse involvement (lacrimal gland, fat, muscle); rapid response to oral steroids.
Pulsatile proptosis; corkscrew epibulbar vessels; orbital bruit.
Molding to globe shape; 'salmon-patch' conjunctival lesions; slow progression.
Bilateral lacrimal gland enlargement; infraorbital nerve enlargement.

sections.title: Medical Management Protocol
content: Step 1: Achieve Euthyroidism (Antithyroid drugs, RAI, or Surgery).
Step 2: Smoking Cessation (Absolute requirement to reduce progression).
Step 3: Selenium Supplementation (100mcg twice daily for 6 months for mild GO).
Step 4: IV Methylprednisolone (EUGOGO Protocol: 0.5g weekly for 6 wks, then 0.25g for 6 wks; Max 6-8g).
Step 5: Biologicals - Teprotumumab (IGF-1R inhibitor) for significant proptosis/diplopia.
Step 6: Second-line - Mycophenolate Mofetil or Orbital Radiotherapy (20 Gy in 10 fractions).

sections.title: RED FLAGS: Dysthyroid Optic Neuropathy (DON)
content: Decreased Visual Acuity (unexplained by surface)
Afferent Pupillary Defect (RAPD)
New-onset Dyschromatopsia (loss of color vision)
Visual Field defects (Central or Arcuate)
Optic Disc edema or pallor

sections.title: Rehabilitative Surgical Sequence
content: 1. Orbital Decompression: Must be done first (may change alignment/lids).
2. Strabismus Surgery: Performed once alignment is stable for 6 months.
3. Eyelid Recession: To address lid retraction (Müller's muscle/levator).
4. Blepharoplasty: Final aesthetic touch for fat prolapse and skin excess.

sections.title: Recent Advances: Teprotumumab
content: Mechanism: Fully human monoclonal antibody inhibitor of IGF-1R.
Dosing: 10mg/kg first dose, then 20mg/kg every 3 weeks for 7 additional doses.
Evidence: OPTIC trials showed significant reduction in proptosis (mean ~3mm).
Side Effects: Muscle cramps, hyperglycemia, and hearing loss (audiometry monitoring required).

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for the Resident
content: The Rundle Curve: TED has an active phase (6-18 months) followed by a stable burnt-out phase.
Never perform elective surgery in the active phase; only for emergencies like DON.
Radioiodine (RAI) can worsen TED; cover with oral Prednisone (0.5mg/kg/day) if needed.
Superior Limbic Keratoconjunctivitis (SLK) is frequently associated with TED.
